summary: Specifies identifiers and challenges so ACME can issue certificates for email users who want S/MIME. A user proves control of an email address to get a certificate.

eli5.summary: Prove you own an email address and receive a digital ID for signing and locking your messages.

questions: how to validate email address for acme
how does acme issue s/mime certificates
subtitle: Automated certificate issuance for email signing and encryption.

tldr.problem: Email users want to sign and encrypt messages with S/MIME, but obtaining and managing certificates for these purposes is manual and cumbersome.
tldr.mechanism: ACME is extended with an email identifier type and an email-reply challenge that proves control of an email address by having the user reply to a server-sent email with a token digest.
tldr.outcome: Email users can now automatically request and obtain S/MIME certificates tied to their email addresses without manual intervention.

today: RFC 8823 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the standard for extending ACME to issue S/MIME certificates for email addresses.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) is a protocol for automating certificate issuance. This document extends ACME to support S/MIME certificates for email users.

Traditional ACME uses domain names to prove control of web resources. For S/MIME, a new identifier type called email proves control of an email address. A user requesting an S/MIME certificate demonstrates that they control the email address by responding to a challenge email sent by the certificate authority.

The protocol supports both ACME-aware email clients that integrate certificate issuance, and standalone ACME tools that users can run independently.
sections.eli5: ACME is a system that automatically gives you digital certificates. Now it can give you certificates for your email address instead of just web domains.

sections.title: Certificate Issuance Flow
sections.content:
The issuance process works in these steps:

  1. The user initiates S/MIME certificate issuance through an email client or command-line tool, specifying their email address.
  2. The ACME client sends a request to create a new order with an email identifier type.
  3. The ACME server responds with an email-reply-00 challenge and provides two token parts: token-part2 (received over HTTPS) and a from address for the challenge email.
  4. The ACME server sends a challenge email with the first token part in its subject line, signed with DKIM or S/MIME.
  5. The user's email client retrieves and parses the challenge email. An ACME-aware client does this automatically.
  6. The client concatenates the two token parts and computes the SHA-256 digest of the key authorization.
  7. The user replies with a response email containing the digest in a special block (between -----BEGIN ACME RESPONSE----- and -----END ACME RESPONSE-----).
  8. The ACME client notifies the server that the response has been sent.
  9. The server validates the received response email, checks the DKIM signature, and confirms the token.
  10. If validation succeeds, the client can finalize the order with a Certificate Signing Request and download the issued certificate.
sections.eli5: The server sends you an email with a secret code in it. You reply to that email with the code in a special format, proving you control the address. Then you get your certificate.

sections.title: Challenge and Response Email Formats
sections.content:
The challenge email MUST have:

  • Subject line: ACME: <token-part1> where token-part1 is base64url-encoded (at least 128 bits).
  • From address: The address specified in the challenge object's from field.
  • To address: The requestor's email address.
  • Auto-Submitted header: auto-generated; type=acme.
  • Authentication: Signed with either DKIM (signing the From, To, Subject, and other critical headers) or S/MIME.

The response email MUST have:

  • Subject: A reply to the challenge subject (typically prefixed with Re:).
  • From: The email address requesting the certificate.
  • To: Either the Reply-To address from the challenge or the From address if no Reply-To is present.
  • In-Reply-To: The Message-ID of the challenge email.
  • Body: Contains the base64url-encoded SHA-256 digest between -----BEGIN ACME RESPONSE----- and -----END ACME RESPONSE----- markers.
  • Authentication: DKIM signed by the sending email domain.
sections.eli5: The challenge email has a code in the subject and is digitally signed so you know it's real. Your reply email contains the answer and is also signed.

sections.title: Signing-Only and Encryption-Only Certificates
sections.content:
S/MIME certificates can serve different purposes. The Certificate Signing Request (CSR) can specify key usage restrictions:

  • Signing-only: The CSR includes the key usage extension with only digitalSignature and/or nonRepudiation bits set. These certificates prove authorship of messages.
  • Encryption-only: The CSR includes key usage with only keyEncipherment or keyAgreement bits set. These certificates encrypt messages so only the recipient can read them.
  • Dual-purpose: Absence of key usage extension or presence of both signing and encryption bits results in a certificate suitable for both operations.

This flexibility allows users to request exactly the capabilities they need for their email client and workflow.
sections.eli5: You can ask for a certificate that only signs messages, only encrypts them, or does both. It depends on what you need.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The email-reply-00 challenge demonstrates that an entity controlling the email account's private key also controls that email address. However, this depends on the security of the email system itself.

If an attacker compromises an email account (by obtaining the password or password-equivalent access), they can request S/MIME certificates indistinguishable from the legitimate account owner. Similarly, shared email accounts with multiple authorized users face this risk. Mailing list addresses are not suitable for this challenge type.

The protocol is vulnerable to DNS spoofing of MX or DKIM records, which could allow an attacker to intercept and reply to challenge emails. Use of DNSSEC is recommended but not required for the same reason it is optional in other email-dependent verification systems such as password recovery and two-factor authentication.

Forged challenge emails are mitigated by requiring DKIM or S/MIME signatures. ACME-aware email clients ignore unexpected challenges, and leaked response emails reveal only the SHA-256 hash of the key authorization, not the key authorization itself, limiting information disclosure.
sections.eli5: The security depends on protecting your email password, because anyone who can read your email can request a certificate. DKIM signatures help prove the challenge emails are real.
